en: The Text for Receiving the Five Precepts and the Eight Precepts. Section One:
Chapter on Bowing the Head and Requesting Witness. Chapter One: Chapter on Bowing the Head and Requesting Witness.

The assembly of disciples prostrates and pays homage to the Unsurpassed Seed-Wisdom of the Dharmadhātu and the void; to those who have attained perfect enlightenment by riding upon the form and manifesting the body; to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, the Vaipulya, and the One Vehicle; to the noble ones of the ten stages and the great bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness; to the various deities, lords of the manifest and the hidden within the void; to the Brahmā kings and their retinues of the Form and Formless Heavens; to the world-protecting Śakra and his assisting officials; and to the judicial officials of the netherworld and Yamarāja, the Lord of Death.
I only pray that today, with the pure divine eye, you shall behold all these people, who with reverent devotion and sincere single-mindedness offer this invocation.

Chapter Two: Washing Away and Repenting of Past Karmic Deeds. The assembly of disciples and those present at the ritual site have, from time immemorial until this day, accumulated immeasurable sins whose boundaries are difficult to fathom; transgressions committed over successive lifetimes are rarely fully investigated.
They give rise to a lack of faith toward the Triple Gem; in the presence of the Honored Ones of the ten directions, they engage in unchaste conduct.
They indulge their bodies in killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; they indulge their speech in lying, frivolous talk, and harsh abuse; and they indulge their minds in greed, anger, and delusion.

From this, boundless evil karma extensively arises; one circulates through the three realms of existence and sinks into the four currents. The five hindrances cover the mind and the ten entanglements delude one's nature; thus one dwells long among the ranks of ordinary beings with no prospect of liberation.

In Sanskrit, *kṣamā* means "to repent" or "to atone for errors. From this day forward, I shall sever the continuity of such thoughts; may all past transgressions and faults be entirely extinguished. Chapter Three: Receiving the Precepts and Taking Refuge in the Triple Gem.

The assembly of disciples and those present at the ritual site together take refuge in the Buddha, the Honored One among Two-legged Beings; they take refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One who is Free from Desire; they take refuge in the Saṃgha, the Honored One among the Multitude. I pray that the Triple Gem, out of compassion, will bear witness, have pity, and graciously accept me. (Recite three times.)

The assembly of disciples and all those present at this ritual site have completed their refuge in the Buddha, completed their refuge in the Dharma, and completed their refuge in the Saṅgha. I now receive the eight precepts of the Upavāsa discipline; may the Honored One remember me and protect me with compassion. (Recite three times.)
Chapter Four: Inquiry into Upholding and Expounding the Teachings. O Sons of the Buddha, listen attentively: what are called the eight precepts are as follows:

first, not killing; second, not stealing; third, not engaging in sexual desire; fourth, not speaking falsely; fifth, not drinking alcohol or eating meat; sixth, not anointing the body with fragrant oils or adorning it with garlands and flowers; seventh, not going to witness or listen to performances of singing, dancing, or music; and eighth, not using high or large beds, nor eating past midday.

Beginning from this moment until the clear dawn of tomorrow morning, for one day and one night, you shall follow the Buddha in renunciation; during this interval, you must not commit any transgression.
Are you able to uphold this?

Chapter Five: Dedication and Aspiration The assembly of disciples and all those gathered at the site of practice take these roots of goodness from receiving the precepts and dedicate them entirely to all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm. May their deluded attachments be dispelled, may the obstacles of ignorance be exhausted, and may non-conceptual wisdom manifest clearly before them. May they ardently cultivate and study the gates of practice with signs, traverse the Flower Treasury World, and profoundly realize the fundamental mind of the Tathāgata-garbha. May those who have not yet realized attain realization, and those who are not yet perfected reach perfection; in the ocean of sentient beings, may all universally aspire to achieve Buddhahood.

The Text on the Five Precepts: All ordinary beings are deluded regarding their fundamental enlightened nature; following along with delusions, they transmigrate through the three realms of existence, resulting in the differentiation of the six destinies and the separation between humans and devas.
The Buddha has established five precepts for people to uphold, entering the principle of true reality through the gate of skillful means.

Chapter One: A Sincere Petition. The assembly of disciples and those gathered at the site of practice together look up and address those who have attained Perfect Enlightenment throughout the ten directions, within the void dharma-realm; those who turn the wheel of Dharma; and those who enter parinirvāṇa. These are our true and virtuous spiritual friends, for the Great Master, the King of Physicians, has taken us under his care.

The boundless treasury of Dharma, the single flavor of the finest cream, the Mahāyāna teaching of the full and partial sounds, is my excellent medicine and my vessel; for it delivers me across the river of birth and death.

The noble assembly of the three vehicles—the eight classes of bhikṣus, the śrāvakas who have entered tranquility, and the bodhisattvas who possess compassion—give rise to a heart of pity for those such as us, just as one who cares for the sick protects and rescues them.
I only pray that the power of the great vows and the inconceivable power of the Triple Gem will give rise to unconditioned compassion within the true nature and accept our invitation this very day.

Chapter Two: Repenting of Previous Sins. The assembly of disciples and those present at the site of practice have been ignorant and deluded throughout kalpas until this day. Because they did not clearly understand the primary truth (*paramārtha*), various gates of obstruction arose—afflictions (*kleśa*) and cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). They were deluded regarding both phenomena and principle; encountering objects, they gave rise to karma, and following conditions, they committed transgressions. From their bodies, the three branches [of misconduct] arose; from their mouths, the four faults were committed; and the three karmic actions of the mind became increasingly deep. Like grains of sand or particles of dust, their number was immeasurable.

One fails to realize that the casket of the body contains four venomous snakes, five caṇḍālas, and the six sense bases as an empty village; one encounters numerous evil conditions that feign intimacy and kindness, driving the conscious mind to wander and revolve through the five destinies.
From this point on, throughout eighty-four thousand human lifetimes, there was no evil I have not committed;
having accumulated these transgressions, today I first examine my body and mind and, appearing before the Buddha, I universally vow that they all be extinguished.

Chapter Three: Turning Away from the Erroneous and Taking Refuge. All disciples and those assembled at the ritual site take refuge in the Buddha, the Unsurpassed Honored One; take refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One Free from Desire; take refuge in the Sangha, the Honored One Among the Multitude.

From this day forward, taking the Buddha as my teacher, I shall no longer turn to other demons, heretics, or external paths; I only pray that the Three Jewels, through their compassion, will bear witness, take pity on me, and accept me—thus three times.
The assembly of disciples and those present at the site of practice have completed their refuge in the Buddha, completed their refuge in the Dharma, and completed their refuge in the Saṃgha.
This Buddha—Bhagavān, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—is my Great Teacher; I now take refuge in him. May the Buddha graciously accept me. (Recite three times.)
Chapter Four: Explaining the Characteristics of Combined Practice. Listen attentively, O Son of the Buddha: what is called the Upāsaka precepts consists of:
first, not killing; second, not stealing; third, no sexual misconduct; fourth, no false speech; and fifth, no drinking of alcohol or eating of meat.
Beginning from this moment until the end of the future, you must not commit any transgression during that interval.
Can you maintain this?

Chapter Five: The Ocean of Vows for Dedication. The assembly of disciples and those present at the ritual site have together received the precepts; they now dedicate them toward the ocean of the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) and bodhi.
May all sentient beings within the four currents and the three realms of existence collectively resolve to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra.
May they never sever the lineage of the Buddhas and be born into the family of the Tathāgatas, further using great compassion to reveal and teach this in turn to others.
Having obtained the jewel from within the topknot and found the pearl within the garment, one shall sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) with the universal vow to attain Buddhahood.
*The Text for Receiving the Five Precepts and Eight Precepts*, one fascicle.
